items.caption: Figure 1: The Transformer - model architecture.
items.title: The two-stack data path
items.takeaway: The figure shows the entire model in one picture: two towers of identical layers, each layer built only from attention and a position-wise feed-forward network. Every sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection plus layer normalization. There is no recurrence and no convolution anywhere, so order information has to be injected once, at the bottom of each tower.
items.walkthrough:
**What you are looking at.** This is one diagram of the whole [[transformer|Transformer]]. Data flows bottom to top. There are two towers.

The left tower is the [[encoder-stack|encoder]]. It reads the source sentence. The right tower is the [[decoder-stack|decoder]], and it emits the target sentence.

Around each tower is a grey rounded box. That box is one layer. The "N×" printed beside it means that layer is stacked $N=6$ times, and each of the six copies carries its own weights — the shape repeats, the parameters do not.

**How to read it.** Two drawing conventions first, before the parts. Every arrow in the figure carries a sequence of vectors, one vector per token. Each of those vectors is [[d-model|$d_{model}=512$]] numbers wide, and that width is the same everywhere in the diagram.

Some arrows leave a box, bypass the next box entirely, and rejoin further up at a band marked **Add & Norm**. That bypass is a [[residual-connection|residual connection]]. What the band computes is $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$: the block's input $x$ is added back onto the block's output, and the sum is then passed through [[layer-normalization|layer normalization]].

The second convention is the fan of three arrows entering each attention box. Those three legs are the queries, the keys and the values. Where all three legs come from the same place below, the box is attending to the very sequence it sits in. That case is [[self-attention]].

**Bottom.** *Inputs* enter at the bottom of the left tower. They pass through *Input Embedding*, a learned lookup that turns each token into a vector of 512 dimensions.

The small circle drawn with a sine wave inside it is the fixed [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|sinusoidal]] [[positional-encoding]]. It is fixed, not learned. The $\oplus$ beside it adds that positional vector to the token embedding elementwise — same width in, same width out.

The right tower repeats this same pair of steps at its own bottom, on *Outputs (shifted right)*.

**Left tower.** Two [[sub-layer|sub-layers]], in this order.

First comes [[multi-head-attention|Multi-Head Attention]] over the output of the previous layer, then an Add & Norm. Second comes a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network|Feed Forward]] network, then another Add & Norm.

That feed-forward network is applied at each position separately and identically, with no mixing across positions. Its widths run $512 \to 2048 \to 512$: expand each position's 512-dimensional vector out to 2048, apply ReLU, project back down to 512.

**Right tower.** Three sub-layers rather than two. The extra one sits in the middle.

The first is labelled *Masked* Multi-Head Attention. It is [[masked-decoder-self-attention|decoder self-attention]] carrying [[causal-masking|causal masking]]: the scores a position assigns to later positions are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax. After the softmax those entries are exactly zero, so no position can read from its own future.

The middle box is another Multi-Head Attention, but its three legs no longer come from one place. The two arrows arriving from the top of the left tower are the keys and the values, taken from the final encoder layer. The query arrow comes from below, out of the decoder itself. That split wiring is what the paper calls [[encoder-decoder-attention]].

The third sub-layer is the same Feed Forward block the encoder uses. Each of the three sub-layers gets its own Add & Norm.

**Top.** The decoder's final output is still 512 numbers wide at each position. *Linear* projects those 512 dimensions out to the vocabulary size, producing one score per vocabulary token. [[softmax|Softmax]] then turns each position's scores into *Output Probabilities* for the next token.

That projection matrix is not its own. It is [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|shared]] with both embedding layers, the one at the bottom of the left tower and the one at the bottom of the right.

**Shifted right.** The label on the decoder input means the target sequence is displaced by one position. The consequence is the point of it: position $i$ is fed only tokens that come before $i$.

In training, the full target sequence is fed in at once. The mask is what makes that safe, so every position can be predicted in parallel without any position seeing what it is meant to predict.

At inference the two towers run on different clocks. The encoder runs once over the source sentence. The decoder then runs one step per token, each step consuming its own previous outputs — [[auto-regressive-generation|auto-regressive]] decoding.

terms.definition: The source token sequence entering the encoder, e.g. the sentence to be translated. In the paper's notation this is $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$.
A learned lookup table that turns each input token into a vector of dimension $d_{model}$. The paper multiplies the embedding weights by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$.

The target token sequence fed into the decoder, offset by one position so that the vector at position $i$ is the token at position $i-1$. Combined with masking, this ensures a prediction for position $i$ depends only on known outputs before $i$.
The learned lookup table for target tokens, the decoder-side twin of Input Embedding. It shares its weight matrix with the input embedding and the final pre-softmax Linear layer.

Vectors added to the embeddings at the bottom of each stack so the model knows token order; without them the architecture is order-blind. They have the same dimension $d_{model}$ as the embeddings so the two can be summed.
The small circle drawn with a wave inside is the source of the positional encoding vectors: each dimension is a sine or cosine of the position at a different frequency.
Elementwise addition. Here it adds the positional encoding vector to the token embedding vector, once per stack, at the very bottom.
The annotation beside each grey box meaning the layer inside is repeated N times in sequence. The layers are identical in structure but each has its own parameters.
The outline enclosing one complete encoder layer (left) or decoder layer (right); it is what the N× multiplier applies to.
Encoder self-attention: queries, keys and values all come from the previous encoder layer, so each position can attend to every position in the input.
Decoder self-attention restricted so each position attends only to itself and earlier positions. Illegal (future) connections are set to $-\infty$ in the softmax input.

The encoder-decoder attention sub-layer. Queries come from the previous decoder layer; keys and values come from the encoder stack's output, so every decoder position can attend over all input positions.

terms.term: Arrows from the encoder to the decoder
terms.definition: The two lines running from the top of the left tower into the middle attention block of every decoder layer. They carry the final encoder output, used as the keys and values; the third arrow, from below, carries the queries.

terms.term: Three-arrow fan into an attention box
terms.definition: The three inputs to multi-head attention: queries, keys and values. All three from the same source means self-attention; split sources mean encoder-decoder attention.
The residual addition followed by layer normalization applied around every sub-layer: the output is $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$.
The curved line that routes a sub-layer's input around it and into the Add & Norm box; it is the residual shortcut, so the sub-layer only has to learn a change to its input.
A two-layer fully connected network applied to each position separately and identically, with a ReLU in between: $\mathrm{FFN}(x)=\max(0,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2$.

The learned linear transformation on top of the decoder that maps each $d_{model}$-dimensional output vector to one score per vocabulary token. It shares its weight matrix with the two embedding layers.
Turns the Linear layer's vocabulary scores into a probability distribution over the next token.
The final result at the top: for each decoder position, a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token.
The stack that maps the input symbols to a sequence of continuous representations $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$. It runs once per input sentence and sees the whole input at once.
The stack that generates the output sequence $(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$ one element at a time, conditioned on the encoder output and on the symbols generated so far.
The name of the whole architecture drawn here: an encoder-decoder built entirely from stacked attention and point-wise feed-forward layers, with no recurrence or convolution.
One attention or feed-forward component inside a layer. Each is wrapped in its own residual connection and layer normalization, which is why every coloured box has an Add & Norm above it.

numbers.meaning: The number of times the boxed layer is repeated in each stack. The paper sets N = 6 for both the encoder and the decoder in the base model. The two N× annotations are independent labels but hold the same value here.
Sub-layers per encoder layer: multi-head self-attention, then the position-wise feed-forward network. Counted as the two coloured boxes inside the left grey box.
Sub-layers per decoder layer: masked self-attention, encoder-decoder attention, then feed-forward. The paper describes the middle one as a third sub-layer inserted relative to the encoder layer.
The number of arrows entering each attention box: queries, keys and values. In the decoder's middle attention box, two of them arrive from the encoder and one from below.

The size of the right-shift on the decoder input. Offsetting the output embeddings by one position, together with the mask, makes the prediction at position i depend only on outputs at positions less than i.
The width of every arrow in the diagram. All sub-layers and both embedding layers produce vectors of this dimension; the paper says this uniformity is what makes the residual additions possible.
The inner width of each Feed Forward box: it expands 512 to 2048, applies ReLU, then projects back to 512.
The value the mask writes into the softmax input for forbidden (future) positions inside the Masked Multi-Head Attention box, so those positions get zero attention weight.
The range of wavelengths of the sinusoids feeding the positional-encoding circles; they form a geometric progression across the 512 dimensions.

items.caption: Figure 2: (left) Scaled Dot-Product Attention. (right) Multi-Head Attention consists of several attention layers running in parallel.
items.title: Attention as a wiring diagram
items.takeaway: The figure draws the paper's attention math as data flow. On the left, Equation (1) is laid out box by box: dot the queries against the keys, scale, optionally mask, softmax, then weight the values. On the right, that whole block becomes a reusable unit, run $h$ times in parallel on separately projected copies of Q, K and V, then concatenated and projected once more.
items.walkthrough:
Two block diagrams, drawn side by side. Data flows bottom to top along the arrows. The inputs enter at the bottom, each rounded box is one operation, and the arrow leaving the top carries the output.

The left diagram is one attention function. The right diagram uses that whole function as a component.

### Left: one attention function

This is the picture of $\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$, drawn one operation at a time. The paper's name for it is [[scaled-dot-product-attention|scaled dot-product attention]].

Three inputs sit at the bottom: $Q$, $K$ and $V$. Each is a matrix whose rows are the [[queries-keys-values|queries, keys and values]]. They are packed this way so that many queries go through the same set of matrix multiplies at once.

The lower **MatMul** takes only two of the three inputs, $Q$ and $K$, and computes $QK^{T}$. That product dots every query with every key. The result is one raw score per query-key pair, arranged with one row per query and one column per key.

**Scale** divides every score in that table by the same constant, $\sqrt{d_k}$. The paper's stated reason is that in high dimensions the dot products grow large, and large inputs push softmax into a region where its gradients are small ([[sqrt-dk-scaling]]).

**Mask (opt.)** is drawn as optional because only some of the model's attention layers use it. In the decoder, the scores for future positions are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax. An exponentiated $-\infty$ is zero, so those positions receive no weight at all ([[causal-masking]]).

**SoftMax** then turns each query's row of scores into weights that sum to 1. It acts along each row separately, so every query ends up with its own distribution over the keys.

The upper **MatMul** multiplies those weights by $V$. Follow $V$'s arrow: it runs up the side of the diagram, bypasses the whole scoring column, and joins only here. Values are never scored, only weighted. What leaves the top is a weighted sum of value vectors.

### Right: h of them at once

The right diagram is [[multi-head-attention]]. The whole left-hand diagram appears inside it as a single box, labeled Scaled Dot-Product Attention, and the rest of the picture is what surrounds that box.

$V$, $K$ and $Q$ enter at the bottom, and each one passes through its own **Linear** block first. Those blocks are the learned projections $W^V_i, W^K_i, W^Q_i$ ([[attention-projection-matrices]]). Each projection cuts its input down to a smaller width: queries and keys to $d_k$ dimensions, values to $d_v$.

The faint offset copies drawn behind each box are the figure's device for showing parallelism. The Linear blocks and the Scaled Dot-Product Attention block are each drawn as a stack of identical sheets. The **h** annotation beside the stack says how many sheets there are.

Each sheet is one [[attention-head]]. A head has its own projection weights and computes the left-hand diagram on its own projected copies of $Q$, $K$ and $V$, independently of the others.

That leaves $h$ separate outputs, one per head. **Concat** glues those $h$ output vectors back into a single wide vector, whose width is the $h$ head widths added together. The final **Linear**, the matrix $W^O$, mixes that wide vector back down to the model's working width. The output of the right diagram therefore has the same width as the inputs that entered it.

terms.definition: The title of the left diagram and the name of the paper's attention function: score each query against each key by a dot product, divide by the square root of the key dimension, softmax, then take the weighted sum of values.
The title of the right diagram: h copies of the left-hand attention function run in parallel on differently projected inputs, then concatenated and projected once more.
The query matrix entering at the bottom of both diagrams. Its rows are the query vectors — one per position asking for information — packed together so many queries are computed at once.
The key matrix. Its rows are the key vectors, one per position, advertising what that position holds; queries are matched against keys to produce the attention scores.

The value matrix. Its rows are the value vectors, one per position, holding the content that gets averaged. In the left diagram its arrow runs past the scoring column and joins only at the top MatMul.
Matrix multiplication of Q with K transposed, producing the raw compatibility score for every query-key pair.
Division of every score by the square root of d_k. The paper adds this step to plain dot-product attention so scores stay moderate as d_k grows.

An optional step that sets forbidden scores to negative infinity before the softmax, so those positions receive zero weight. Used in the decoder to block attention to future positions, and skipped in encoder self-attention — hence '(opt.)'.
Turns each query's row of scaled scores into non-negative weights that sum to one, by exponentiating each score and dividing by the row's total.
Matrix multiplication of the softmax weights with V, producing each query's output as a weighted sum of value vectors. This is the output of the attention function.

terms.term: Linear (the three blocks at the bottom right)
terms.definition: Learned linear projections applied to V, K and Q before attention. Each head gets its own projection matrices, mapping d_model-dimensional inputs down to d_k (keys, queries) or d_v (values) dimensions.

terms.term: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (the block in the right diagram)
terms.definition: The entire left-hand diagram reused as a single unit inside multi-head attention. It appears once as a box but is drawn stacked, because it is instantiated once per head.
Concatenation of the h per-head output vectors into one wider vector, of width h times d_v, before the final projection.
The final learned projection W^O applied after Concat, mixing the concatenated head outputs back to d_model width.
The label on the stacked sheets giving how many parallel attention heads there are. It points at the stack to say the depth of that stack is h, not some fixed drawn count.

The faint duplicate outlines drawn behind the Linear and Scaled Dot-Product Attention boxes. They are a drawing convention for 'this same block exists h times, each with its own weights, all running in parallel' — not h sequential layers.
One sheet of the stack: one set of Q/K/V projections plus one scaled dot-product attention computation, producing a d_v-dimensional output per position.
The dimension of each query and key vector inside a head; it sets the scaling factor in the Scale box. Not printed in the figure but it is what Scale divides by.
The dimension of each value vector inside a head, and therefore the width of each head's output before Concat.
The model's working width: what enters the bottom Linear blocks and what leaves the top Linear block, so multi-head attention is width-preserving.
The per-head parameter matrices realized by the three bottom Linear blocks, each of shape d_model by d_k (or d_model by d_v for values).
The parameter matrix realized by the top Linear block, of shape (h times d_v) by d_model, mapping the concatenated head outputs back to model width.
Data flow, running bottom to top. Arrow merges into a box mean that box takes multiple inputs; the multiple thin arrows into Concat are the h head outputs.

numbers.meaning: The number of parallel attention heads, marked by the annotation on the stacked sheets. Left symbolic in the figure; the paper sets it to 8 for its models.
The head count actually used in the paper's models: eight parallel attention layers.

The per-head key/query and value dimensions. Each head works in a reduced space so that, as the paper puts it, the total computational cost is about the same as one attention function at full dimensionality.
The base model's width — the size of vectors entering the bottom Linear blocks and leaving the top one. With h = 8 this gives the 64 above.

The factor applied in the Scale box. The paper's reason: for large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude and push softmax into regions of extremely small gradients. It notes that if query and key components were independent with mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product would have mean 0 and variance d_k.
The concrete divisor in the paper's base model, following from d_k = 64. The figure itself only says 'Scale'.
The value the Mask box writes into forbidden score entries, so that after SoftMax those positions get weight zero. Not printed in the figure; it is how the paper implements the mask.
Each query's softmax weights sum to one, which is what makes the top MatMul a weighted average of value vectors rather than an arbitrary combination.
The number of Linear blocks along the bottom of the right diagram — one each for V, K and Q. Every head has its own copy of all three.
The number of MatMul boxes in the left diagram: the first for Q against K transposed, the second for the softmax weights against V.
There is only one projection after Concat, shared across heads, unlike the three per-head projections below.
The width of the vector leaving Concat, and therefore the input width of the final Linear block. With h = 8 and d_v = 64 this equals 512, matching d_model.
The numbered equation in the paper that the left diagram draws: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.

items.caption: Table 1: Maximum path lengths, per-layer complexity and minimum number of sequential operations for different layer types. n is the sequence length, d is the representation dimension, k is the kernel size of convolutions and r the size of the neighborhood in restricted self-attention.
items.title: Layer types by cost and path length
items.takeaway: The table is the paper's argument for replacing recurrence with self-attention. A self-attention layer connects every position to every other in a constant number of sequential steps, over a path of length 1, where a recurrent layer needs $O(n)$ of both. Its per-layer arithmetic cost, $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, is lower than a recurrent layer's $O(n \cdot d^2)$ whenever the sequence is shorter than the model is wide.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at a four-row comparison. Each row is one way to build a single layer that maps a sequence $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of $d$-dimensional vectors to another sequence $(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ of the same length and the same width. That is the shape of a hidden layer inside a [[sequence-transduction|sequence transduction]] encoder or decoder, so the four rows are four candidates for the same slot in the same architecture.

Four symbols carry every entry in the table. $n$ is the sequence length, the number of tokens. $d$ is the representation dimension; in the paper's base model that is [[d-model|$d_{model}=512$]]. $k$ is the kernel width of a convolution. $r$ is the neighborhood size in [[restricted-self-attention|restricted self-attention]], which is the last row.

Take the columns before the rows. They are the paper's [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three criteria]] for judging a layer type.

[[complexity-per-layer|Complexity per layer]] is the total arithmetic one layer performs.

[[minimum-sequential-operations|Sequential operations]] counts the steps that must run one after another, because a later step needs an earlier step's output. It is therefore a measure of what cannot be parallelized, however much hardware is available.

[[maximum-path-length|Maximum path length]] is the longest hop count a signal travels between any two positions, going forward or coming back as gradient. Shorter paths, the paper says, make [[long-range-dependencies|long-range dependencies]] easier to learn.

One caveat before reading any value. Every entry is big-O in $n$, $d$, $k$ and $r$ — asymptotic operation counts, not measured speed. Lower is better in all three columns.

Now the first row. [[self-attention|Self-attention]] compares every position with every other, which is $n \times n = n^2$ pairs, and each comparison is a dot product over $d$ dimensions. That gives the $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ arithmetic in the first column. The other two columns are where it pays off: $O(1)$ sequential operations and $O(1)$ path length. One layer already puts every position a single hop from every other.

Second row. A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent]] layer costs $O(n \cdot d^2)$, which is $n$ time steps, each one a $d \times d$ matrix multiply, and a $d \times d$ multiply is $d^2$ work. But it is $O(n)$ in both of the remaining columns, because step $t$ cannot start until step $t-1$ has produced its hidden state ([[sequential-computation-bottleneck|the bottleneck]]). Information from the first position reaches the last only by being handed along all $n$ steps.

The two cost expressions cross over somewhere. Set $n^2 d$ against $n d^2$ and divide both by $n d$; what remains is $n$ against $d$. So self-attention is the cheaper layer exactly when $n < d$ — when the sequence is shorter than the model is wide. The paper says this is most often the case for sentences tokenized with [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] or [[byte-pair-encoding|byte-pair]] vocabularies.

That leaves the two rows that qualify the picture rather than headline it.

[[convolutional-sequence-models|Convolutional]] layers match self-attention on parallelism, at $O(1)$ sequential operations. Their per-layer cost is a factor of $k$ above the recurrent layer's, that is $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$, since each output position mixes $k$ input positions rather than one. And a single layer with $k < n$ does not connect all pairs: its receptive field is only $k$ wide. Reaching across the whole sequence takes a stack — $O(n/k)$ layers with contiguous kernels, or $O(\log_k n)$ with [[dilated-convolutions|dilated convolutions]], which widen the span each layer covers.

The last row is a proposal, not a trained model. Restrict each position to attend only within a neighborhood of $r$ positions around it. Cost falls to $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$, because each of the $n$ positions now scores $r$ keys instead of $n$. The price shows up in the path column: information moves at most $r$ positions per layer, so crossing the sequence stretches to $O(n/r)$ hops.

terms.definition: The row header column: each row is one candidate design for a single sequence-to-sequence layer being compared on equal footing.
Total arithmetic performed by one layer, written as a big-O function of n, d, k, r. Lower means cheaper compute per layer.
The minimum number of operations that must execute one after another inside the layer, i.e. what cannot be parallelized across positions. The paper's proxy for parallelizability.
The longest number of network hops a forward or backward signal must traverse between any input position and any output position. Shorter is claimed to make long-range dependencies easier to learn.
Row 1: a layer where every position attends to every other position of the same sequence. All pairs are connected within a single layer.
Row 2: a layer that walks the sequence position by position, carrying a hidden state forward, as in an LSTM or GRU.
Row 3: a layer that applies a width-k kernel over the sequence, mixing each position with its k-neighborhood in parallel.
Row 4: a proposed variant, not used in the paper's trained models, where each output position attends only to the r input positions around it instead of all n.
Sequence length: the number of tokens or positions in the input sequence, which equals the number of output positions here.
Representation dimension: the width of the vector held at each position. In the paper's base Transformer this is d_model = 512.
Kernel size (width) of a convolution: how many neighboring positions one convolution filter spans.
Neighborhood size in restricted self-attention: each output position attends only to the r input positions centered on it.
Asymptotic order-of-growth notation. Every cell states how a quantity scales with n, d, k, r as they grow, ignoring constant factors — it is not a measured runtime.
Logarithm of the sequence length in base k: how many layers of dilated convolutions with kernel width k are needed before every pair of positions is connected.
From the surrounding text: the input and output vectors at position i, both in R^d. The layer maps (x_1,...,x_n) to (z_1,...,z_n) of equal length.

numbers.meaning: Self-attention's complexity per layer. Quadratic in n because each of n positions computes a compatibility score against all n positions, and each score involves d-dimensional vectors.
Recurrent layer's complexity per layer. n sequential steps, each applying a d x d weight matrix to a d-dimensional state, which costs d^2.

Convolutional layer's complexity per layer. The same d x d mixing at each of n positions as a recurrent layer, but repeated across the k kernel taps — the paper states convolutions are generally more expensive than recurrent layers by a factor of k.
Restricted self-attention's complexity per layer. Each of n positions attends to only r neighbors instead of all n, so n^2 in the first row becomes r · n.

The sequential-operations entry for self-attention, convolutional, and restricted self-attention: a constant number of steps regardless of sequence length, because all positions are computed in parallel. Also self-attention's maximum path length — any two positions are connected directly in one layer.

Appears twice in the recurrent row: n sequential operations (step t cannot start until step t-1 finishes) and a maximum path length of n (a signal must pass through up to n recurrent steps to reach a distant position). These two n's are why the paper wants to replace recurrence.
Convolutional maximum path length. One layer with kernel width k < n does not connect all pairs; the text says a stack of dilated convolutions reaches all pairs in log base k of n layers.
Restricted self-attention's maximum path length: with a window of r, reaching a position n away takes about n/r hops. This is the cost the paper flags for the cheaper first column.
Not in the table but in the text: the number of stacked contiguous-kernel convolutional layers needed to connect all pairs of positions, the non-dilated alternative to O(log_k(n)).
The only exponents in the table. n^2 comes from all-pairs attention scoring; d^2 comes from a full d x d linear map applied per position. Which one dominates is the whole comparison.

The condition under which self-attention is cheaper per layer than recurrence, since O(n^2 · d) < O(n · d^2) exactly when n < d. The paper says this is most often the case for sentence representations built from word-piece or byte-pair vocabularies.
From elsewhere in the paper, not printed in the table: the base model's d_model. It gives a concrete sense of the n < d threshold — typical subword-tokenized sentences are shorter than 512 tokens.
The regime the text discusses for convolutions: when the kernel is narrower than the sequence, a single convolutional layer cannot connect all input-output pairs, hence the need for a stack.

The text's limiting case: even with a kernel spanning the whole sequence, a separable convolution's complexity equals that of a self-attention layer plus a point-wise feed-forward layer — the combination the Transformer actually uses.
Not in the table but cited in the text: the complexity of separable convolutions, which the paper says reduces the convolutional cost considerably relative to O(k · n · d^2).
The stated ratio by which ordinary convolutional layers are more expensive than recurrent layers — the difference between O(k · n · d^2) and O(n · d^2).
The number of criteria the section compares, which is the number of non-header columns in the table: per-layer complexity, minimum sequential operations, and maximum path length.

The number of layer types compared: self-attention, recurrent, convolutional, and restricted self-attention. Only the first three are used in real models here; the fourth is a proposal for very long sequences left to future work.

items.caption: Table 2: The Transformer achieves better BLEU scores than previous state-of-the-art models on the English-to-German and English-to-French newstest2014 tests at a fraction of the training cost.
items.title: Translation quality against training cost
items.takeaway: On the WMT 2014 newstest2014 benchmarks, the big Transformer reports the best English-to-German BLEU in the table: 28.4, more than 2.0 BLEU above every earlier model listed, ensembles included. Its English-to-French score is competitive rather than best. And its estimated training cost is at least a few times lower than any competitive baseline. The base Transformer, at roughly 3.3e18 FLOPs, already scores above every prior row on English-to-German.
items.walkthrough:
The table holds ten translation systems, one per row. Every one of them is scored on the same two test sets, which is what makes the rows comparable at all.

There are four value columns, and they come in two pairs. Reading them as two pairs rather than as four separate columns is the key to the table.

The left pair is [[bleu|BLEU]] score. One column is WMT 2014 English-to-German ([[wmt-2014-en-de|EN-DE]]), the other is English-to-French ([[wmt-2014-en-fr|EN-FR]]). Both are measured on the newstest2014 test set. Higher is better, and on these particular benchmarks a gap of a single point is considered large.

The right pair is not quality at all. It is the estimated cost of *training* that model, measured in floating-point operations, given once for each language pair.

Two conventions govern the cells themselves. A blank cell means that system never reported that number — it is missing data, not a zero. A bracketed number is a citation to the original paper the row came from.

### The three blocks

Horizontal rules split the ten rows into three groups.

The top block is prior single models. [[bytenet|ByteNet]] is a dilated-convolution translator. Deep-Att + PosUnk is a deep recurrent net with fast-forward connections, combined with a rare-word fix — "PosUnk" is the "position unknown" handling for words the model cannot produce directly. GNMT + RL is Google's production LSTM system, fine-tuned with reinforcement learning. [[convs2s|ConvS2S]] is a fully convolutional seq2seq model. MoE is an LSTM carrying a sparsely gated mixture-of-experts layer, which activates only a few experts per input rather than the whole layer — that selective spending of compute is [[conditional-computation]].

The middle block is [[model-ensembling|ensembles]] of three of those same systems. An ensemble is several separately trained copies of a model decoding together. It is a routine way to buy 1–2 BLEU, and the price is several times the compute.

The bottom block is the paper's own two configurations, the [[base-vs-big-transformer|base and big]] [[transformer|Transformer]].

### Where the cost numbers come from

The cost column is not a measurement. It comes from a rough formula ([[training-flops-estimate]]): training time, multiplied by the number of GPUs, multiplied by an assumed sustained single-precision throughput per GPU.

That last factor is a lookup, not an observation. Footnote 5 gives the assumed rates: 2.8 TFLOPS for a K80, 3.7 for a K40, 6.0 for an M40, and 9.5 for a P100.

Now walk the base model's entry. It trained on [[training-hardware-and-schedule|8 P100s for 12 hours]]. Twelve hours is 43,200 seconds. So the estimate is $8 \times 43{,}200\,\text{s} \times 9.5\times10^{12} \approx 3.3\times10^{18}$.

The same arithmetic runs for the big model, with 3.5 days in place of 12 hours. That gives $2.3\times10^{19}$.

Note what the 9.5 in that product actually is. It is nominal capacity, not measured utilization. So the whole column should be treated as an order-of-magnitude figure.

### Two things to watch in the printing

Bold marks the best value in a column. In the EN-FR column, two entries are bold: 41.29 and 41.8.

There is a second inconsistency alongside it. The running text quotes 41.0 for the big model, not the 41.8 printed here. Both look like leftovers from a revision of that number.

One last caveat covers the whole table. The comparison runs across papers, so data pipelines and tokenization differ between rows. The paper reports only what previous work published.

The claim the table is built to support: a single Transformer beats prior ensembles on EN-DE, while costing about an order of magnitude less to train than the ensembles it beats.

items.title: One-knob-at-a-time ablations
items.takeaway: Table 3 changes one design choice of the base Transformer at a time and reports the effect on English-to-German development-set quality. It shows a middling head count (around 8-16) is best, shrinking the attention key dimension $d_k$ hurts, bigger models are better, and dropout matters a lot. Learned positional embeddings match sinusoids almost exactly, so this table does not choose between them.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

An ablation table for [[transformer-ablations|the Transformer's design choices]]. Every row is one separately trained model.

The first row, `base`, is the full base configuration. The last row, `big`, is the scaled-up one. Everything in between falls into groups labelled (A) through (E).

Each row in those groups changes exactly one thing relative to `base`. That is the discipline the whole table rests on: turn one knob, hold the rest fixed, and any difference in the result belongs to that knob.

Most cells in those rows are blank. **A blank cell means "same as base"** — that is what the caption's "unlisted values are identical" is telling you.

### How to read it

The table divides into two blocks. The left block is what was dialled in; the right block is what came out.

The left block, in order: [[n-layers|$N$]], the number of layers in each stack; the model width [[d-model|$d_{model}$]]; the feed-forward inner width [[d-ff|$d_{ff}$]]; the number of [[multi-head-attention|attention heads]] [[num-heads-h|$h$]]; the per-head key and value sizes [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k$ and $d_v$]]; the [[residual-dropout|dropout rate]] $P_{drop}$; the [[label-smoothing|label smoothing]] amount $\epsilon_{ls}$; and the number of training steps.

The right block is shorter: [[perplexity|PPL]], [[bleu|BLEU]], and the parameter count in millions. Lower PPL is better, higher BLEU is better.

Now the measurement conditions, which matter before comparing any of these numbers to anything outside the table. All results are on newstest2013, the English-German development set. Decoding uses [[beam-search]]. It does not use [[checkpoint-averaging]], which the paper does apply to its headline translation results.

One caveat about the PPL column in particular. It is measured **per word-piece** under the paper's [[byte-pair-encoding|byte-pair encoding]], not per word. A model predicting sub-word pieces is making more, individually easier predictions, so these perplexities are not comparable to per-word perplexities reported elsewhere.

### What it shows

Group (A) sweeps the head count $h$, and adjusts the per-head width to compensate, following the rule $d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$.

Work that rule through. $d_{model}$ is 512, and the base setting uses 8 heads, so each head gets $512/8 = 64$ dimensions. Push up to 32 heads and each one gets $512/32 = 16$. Collapse down to a single head and it gets all 512 to itself.

Because the per-head width shrinks exactly as fast as the head count grows, the total attention computation stays roughly constant across the sweep. The comparison is therefore about how a fixed budget is divided, not how large the budget is.

[[attention-heads-ablation|Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU below the best setting]]: 24.9 against 25.8. Quality also drops at the other end of the sweep, with 32 heads scoring 25.4.

Both extremes lose. The good settings sit in the middle.

Group (B) changes $d_k$ alone, leaving $d_v$ at 64. This is not the compute trade of group (A); it isolates how much room the query-key match itself has to work in.

[[key-size-ablation|Quality falls]]. The function that scores a query against a key, and whose scores become the attention weights, is the [[compatibility-function|compatibility function]]; in this model it is a plain [[dot-product-attention|dot product]]. The paper suggests that this may be too simple, and that the compatibility function may need to be more than a dot product.

Groups (C) and (D) confirm the expected: [[size-and-dropout-ablation|bigger is better, and dropout helps]]. Group (C) scales the model up along $N$, $d_{model}$, and $d_{ff}$; group (D) varies the regularization.

The dropout effect is the sharper of the two. Removing dropout entirely, setting $P_{drop}=0.0$, costs 1.2 BLEU.

Row (E) swaps the [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|sinusoids]] for [[learned-positional-embedding|learned positional embeddings]], leaving everything else at base.

The results come out near-identical: 4.92 PPL and 25.7 BLEU, against base's 25.8 BLEU. Translation quality does not distinguish the two schemes.

Which is why the paper's preference for sinusoids rests on grounds this table does not measure.

items.title: The parsing leaderboard
items.takeaway: Trained on the ~40K-sentence WSJ treebank with almost no task-specific tuning, a 4-layer Transformer reaches 91.3 F1 on WSJ Section 23. That is above every listed discriminative parser except Dyer et al.'s RNN Grammar at 91.7. Adding the ~17M auto-parsed sentences takes it to 92.7, the best semi-supervised number in the table — and in both regimes it beats the RNN sequence-to-sequence parser (Vinyals & Kaiser et al.) whose experimental setup it borrows.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at a small leaderboard for [[constituency-parsing|English constituency parsing]]. The task is to predict a sentence's syntactic tree — the nesting of phrases inside phrases. This is the paper's only experiment that is not translation.

Its purpose is to test whether [[transformer|the Transformer]] transfers to a different kind of [[sequence-transduction|sequence transduction]] task. Parsing differs from translation in two ways that matter here. The output is longer than the input, and the output must obey hard structural constraints rather than merely reading well.

### How to read it

The table has three columns. **Parser** names the system and its citation. **Training** names the data regime that system was trained under. **WSJ 23 F1** is the score.

Every entry in that last column is measured the same way. So the numbers can be read straight down the column and compared.

That measurement is worth unpacking, because *F1 here* is not the classification F1. It is the parsing-evaluation F1, the one computed by EVALB. Start with the predicted tree and the gold tree for a sentence. From each of them, list every labelled constituent — a span of the sentence together with its label, e.g. `NP(3,7)`, a noun phrase covering words 3 through 7.

Then compare the two lists. Precision is the fraction of predicted constituents that also appear in the gold tree. Recall is the fraction of gold constituents that the prediction recovered.

The two are combined in the usual way, $F_1 = 2PR/(P+R)$. It is reported here on a 0–100 scale rather than 0–1.

The column header also names the test data. Section 23 of the [[penn-treebank-wsj|Penn Treebank WSJ]] is the standard held-out test split for this task. A number in this column is therefore comparable to any other published Section 23 figure.

Now the rows. Horizontal rules divide the table into blocks by training regime, and the blocks are not comparable to one another.

The first block is *WSJ only, discriminative*. These systems are trained on the roughly 40K hand-parsed sentences of the treebank. Discriminative means they score trees directly, rather than also modelling the probability of the sentence itself.

The second block is [[semi-supervised-parsing|semi-supervised]]. Same 40K-sentence treebank, plus roughly 17M sentences that were parsed automatically rather than by hand. That is over 400 times as much data as the treebank, none of it verified by a human.

The last two rows sit outside both blocks. One is multi-task, one is generative. Treat them as context rather than like-for-like comparisons.

### What it shows

The Transformer rows are the ones to anchor on. It scores 91.3 in the WSJ-only regime and 92.7 in the semi-supervised regime.

Take the WSJ-only block first. 91.3 puts the Transformer above [[berkeley-parser|the BerkeleyParser]] (Petrov et al., 90.4), and above Zhu et al., also at 90.4.

It falls below exactly one system in that block: [[recurrent-neural-network-grammar|the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar]] of Dyer et al., at 91.7. That is the single exception the paper names.

In the semi-supervised block there is no such exception. 92.7 is the top number in the block.

One row deserves separate attention, because it appears in both blocks: Vinyals & Kaiser et al. That is the [[recurrent-neural-network|RNN]] sequence-to-sequence parser whose experimental setup the Transformer copies.

Copying the setup makes it the closest thing to a controlled comparison the table offers. The Transformer beats it by 3.0 F1 in the WSJ-only regime, so 91.3 against 88.3. In the semi-supervised regime the margin narrows to 0.6 F1, 92.7 against 92.1.

That leaves the question of how much of this came from tuning. The paper stresses that only three things were tuned for parsing: dropout rates, learning rate, and [[beam-search|beam]] size. Those were chosen on the Section 22 development set, not on the Section 23 test set the table reports.

Everything else was left at the English-German base translation settings.

So the claim these numbers support is generalization, not a tuned parsing result.

items.caption: Figure 3: An example of the attention mechanism following long-distance dependencies in the encoder self-attention in layer 5 of 6. Many of the attention heads attend to a distant dependency of the verb ‘making’, completing the phrase ‘making...more difficult’. Attentions here shown only for the word ‘making’. Different colors represent different heads. Best viewed in color.
items.title: Heads tracking "making … more difficult"
items.takeaway: This is one query word's attention pattern in a single encoder self-attention layer, drawn as lines running from that word to the positions it attends to, each line colored by the head that produced it. Several of the eight heads put most of their weight on "more" and "difficult", six and seven tokens away from "making". The paper offers this as an illustration that self-attention can link distant, grammatically related words in a single step.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

The figure shows the attention of a single query position, taken from a Transformer that has already been trained. The layer it comes from is an [[encoder-self-attention|encoder self-attention]] layer — specifically layer 5 out of the [[n-layers|six]] stacked layers in the encoder.

The input is one English sentence: *"It is in this spirit that a majority of American governments have passed new laws since 2009 making the registration or voting process more difficult."*

That sentence is written out twice in the figure, once along the top edge and once along the bottom edge. Both copies are the same sentence in the same word order. The words are rotated to run vertically only so that they fit in the width of the page; the rotation carries no meaning.

The sequence is padded out to a fixed length before it enters the model. After the final word comes an `<EOS>` marker, and after that come six `<pad>` slots. The sentence itself is 26 tokens; add the one `<EOS>` and the six `<pad>` slots and you get the 33 positions that make up the columns of the figure.

### How to read it

The two copies of the sentence play different roles. The top copy holds the *querying* positions — the words doing the looking. The bottom copy holds the positions being *attended to* — the words being looked at.

Only one query is drawn here, so the top row is almost entirely inactive. The single active query is the word "making", marked by the gray box in the top row. Every line in the figure leaves that box.

Each line ends on a word in the bottom row, and it means that "making" assigned some attention weight to that word. The opacity of the line encodes how much weight. Those weights are a [[softmax]] output, which means that within any one head the weights across all 33 positions sum to 1. So a faint line is a small share of that budget, and a solid line is a large share.

The color of a line tells you which [[attention-head|head]] produced it. The model does not run one attention function over the full-width vectors; it runs [[num-heads-h|eight]] of them side by side, each on its own separately projected copy of the queries, keys and values. That arrangement is [[multi-head-attention]]. Because each head computes its own softmax over the 33 positions, each head has its own distribution — and therefore its own color in the figure.

The colored cells stacked underneath the bottom sentence carry exactly the same numbers in a different form. Read them as a heat strip: one row per head, one column per word, and shade standing in for weight.

### What it shows

Now to the pattern itself. Most of the visible weight lands on just two words out of the 33 positions available.

Four heads — blue, orange, green and gray — concentrate on "more". Four heads — blue, green, red and brown — concentrate on "difficult". Both of those words sit well to the right of the query: "more" is six tokens after "making" and "difficult" is seven, with the phrase "the registration or voting process" filling the gap between them.

Not every head joins in. A purple head attends back to "making" itself, and a pink head attends to "2009" and to "laws".

The paper reads the dominant pattern as heads following the verb out to its complement. "Making" and "more difficult" belong together grammatically, and the heads span the intervening phrase to connect them.

That connection is made in one attention hop rather than the six sequential steps a position-by-position model would need to cover the same distance. This is the [[maximum-path-length]] argument, shown on a concrete sentence: a [[long-range-dependencies|long-distance dependency]] closed in a single layer.

Treat the figure as an example rather than a measurement. Nothing here is quantified over a corpus, and the paper itself only says that the attention distributions [[attention-interpretability|appear to relate]] to the structure of the sentence.

items.caption: Figure 4: Two attention heads, also in layer 5 of 6, apparently involved in anaphora resolution. Top: Full attentions for head 5. Bottom: Isolated attentions from just the word ‘its’ for attention heads 5 and 6. Note that the attentions are very sharp for this word.
items.title: Two heads that resolve "its"
items.takeaway: Two different attention heads in the same encoder layer put almost all of the word "its" attention on two different words — head 5 on "Law", head 6 on "application". The paper offers this as a sign that individual heads pick up distinct, sentence-structure-related jobs. Here that job is apparently anaphora resolution, which nobody supervised or programmed.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Both panels show attention weights pulled out of one trained [[transformer|Transformer]]. The sentence fed to it is English: *"The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just — this is what we are missing, in my opinion."*

The weights come from [[encoder-self-attention|encoder self-attention]]. That places them in the encoder, whose stack is 6 layers deep, and specifically at layer 5 of those 6. Self-attention means the queries and the keys come from the same sequence, so every token here is attending to tokens of this one sentence and nothing else.

The word under examination is *its*. Working out what a pronoun points back to has a name: *anaphora resolution*. In this sentence the question is whose application, and the answer is the Law's.

Nothing in the training objective asks the model to answer that question. It was trained to translate.

### How to read the panels

Each panel prints the same sentence twice, once above and once below. The **top row is the querying positions**. The **bottom row is the attended positions**.

A line drawn from a token on top to a token on the bottom means the top token's [[queries-keys-values|query]] put weight on the bottom token's [[queries-keys-values|key]]. The size of that weight is drawn two ways at once: darker lines and thicker lines mean more weight.

Those weights are the output of a [[softmax]], so they are a distribution. The consequence for reading the picture: all the lines leaving any single top token sum to 1. A token that spends weight in one place has none left to spend elsewhere.

**Top panel.** This is all of head 5's attention at once — every query position in the sentence, drawn together. Most of what you see is faint, which means most queries spread their weight thinly across many positions. A handful of dark lines stand out against that background.

**Bottom panel.** Same picture, stripped down. Everything is removed except the lines leaving the single word *its*, which is shaded grey to mark it as the query. What is added is a second head: the panel now shows two heads at once, purple for head 5 and tan for head 6.

The two colors go to two different places. Head 5 sends nearly all of *its* weight to **Law**. Head 6 sends nearly all of it to **application**.

The stacked bars drawn under those two words are the per-head accounting — each head's share of the weight it gave that word. The caption describes the attentions as "very sharp" for this word. Sharp here means concentrated on a single position rather than smeared across many.

### What it shows

The same input, the same depth in the stack, two [[attention-head|heads]] — and different behaviour. That is the observation the figure is built to make.

The paper's reading of the observation is hedged, and the hedge is in its own words: the heads are "apparently involved in anaphora resolution". This is one sentence and one pronoun. It is an example, not a measurement.

Taken as an example, it supports the broader point Section 4 makes: [[attention-interpretability|inspecting attention distributions]] suggests that individual heads learn separate tasks. That in turn is part of the case for [[multi-head-attention]] rather than a single attention function whose one weighted average would have to serve both purposes at once.

items.title: Two heads, one sentence
items.takeaway: Two attention heads from the same encoder self-attention layer, run on the same sentence, produce visibly different attention patterns. One fans many positions into a few words; the other makes sparse, short, word-to-word links. The paper offers this as a qualitative illustration that heads specialize, and says only that the patterns "seem related" to sentence structure — nothing here is measured.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two pictures of the same thing.

Each panel shows every attention weight produced by a single [[attention-head|head]] on a single sentence. A head does not emit one number per word. It emits one number for every ordered pair of positions: for each word doing the looking, a weight on each word being looked at. A panel draws that entire grid at once, so every query row and every attended column is present — this is the full attention map of the head, not a slice of it.

The head sits inside the [[encoder-self-attention]] sub-layer at layer 5, out of the encoder's 6 layers.

The input is one sentence: *"The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just - this is what we are missing, in my opinion."*

The top panel is one head, drawn in green. The bottom panel is a different head, taken from that same layer, drawn in red.

Sentence, layer, and model are identical across the two panels. The layer index is doing the work of a control here, not of a claim. So whatever differs between the panels is the difference between the two heads, and nothing else.

### How to read a panel

Each panel prints the sentence twice, once along the top and once along the bottom.

The top copy is the *querying* positions — the words asking for information. The bottom copy is the positions being attended to — the words on offer.

Both copies are the same sentence, and that is exactly what makes this [[self-attention|self-attention]]. The [[queries-keys-values|queries, keys, and values]] all come from the previous encoder layer, so every position is looking only within its own sentence.

A line drawn from a top token to a bottom token is one attention weight. The darker and more opaque the line, the larger that weight.

Opacity is the only quantitative channel in the figure. There are no axes and no printed numbers. Anything read off a panel is therefore a relative judgement about shading, not a measurement.

One constraint does hold exactly, and it is worth keeping in mind while looking. The lines leaving any single top token form a [[softmax]] distribution over the bottom positions, so they sum to 1. A token that sends heavy mass in one direction is necessarily sending less everywhere else.

### What it shows

Start with the green head, in the top panel. It spreads.

A faint haze of lines covers almost every top-to-bottom pair, and sitting on top of that haze are heavy fans converging on a handful of words: *Law*, *application*, *missing*, *opinion*. Many different querying positions are routing their mass into the same few tokens.

That is not one strong weight drawn many times. It is many separate distributions, one per querying position, that happen to agree on where to look.

The red head, in the bottom panel, does close to the opposite. Its links are mostly short and near-vertical: each query picks out one or two specific tokens near it, and there is little background haze behind them.

Two different jobs, in the same layer, at the same time. That is the behaviour [[multi-head-attention]] is meant to make room for.

Now to the claims attached to the figure, which are pitched at deliberately different strengths.

That the heads "learned to perform different tasks" is stated flatly in the caption, and the two panels do show it — the shapes are not subtly different.

That the behaviour relates to sentence structure only "seems" so. The caption hedges that half and does not hedge the first half.

Section 4 keeps the same distance. Heads there "appear to exhibit" behaviour related to syntactic and semantic structure, and [[attention-interpretability|interpretability]] is offered as a side benefit of multi-head attention rather than as a result the paper defends.

The evidence supporting the softer claim is two hand-picked heads on one sentence. There is no syntactic annotation drawn on the figure and no score reported alongside it. Nothing here is measured.

One detail cuts against reading every dark line as linguistic. Both panels carry a dark self-link on `<pad>` — a position holding no word at all.
