items.caption: Scaled dot-product attention, eq. (1)
items.title: The scaled dot-product attention formula
items.takeaway: This is the paper's whole attention function in one line: score every query against every key with a dot product, shrink the scores by $\sqrt{d_k}$, softmax them into weights, and return the weighted sum of the values. The $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor is the only thing separating it from ordinary dot-product attention. The paper adds it because it suspects large dot products push the softmax into regions with very small gradients.
items.walkthrough:
Equation (1) defines [[scaled-dot-product-attention|the attention function]] that the whole Transformer is built from. Every attention layer in the model is a call to this one formula.

It is written for a batch of queries at once. Everything in it is a matrix rather than a single vector, so one call handles a full sequence of positions.

### How to read it

The three inputs are [[queries-keys-values|queries, keys, and values]], packed as the rows of three matrices.

$Q$ holds one row per query, and each of those rows has dimension [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k$]]. $K$ holds one row per key, also of dimension $d_k$. The two dimensions must match, because a query row and a key row are about to be dotted together.

$V$ holds one row per value, of dimension $d_v$. That dimension is free to differ from $d_k$, since values are never dotted against anything.

$K$ and $V$ always have the same number of rows. Keys and values come in pairs: the key is what a position advertises, and the value is the content that position hands over when selected.

Give the two counts names. Say there are $n$ queries and $m$ key-value pairs. Then $Q$ is $n \times d_k$, $K$ is $m \times d_k$, and $V$ is $m \times d_v$.

Now read the formula from the inside out, starting with the innermost product.

$QK^T$ multiplies an $n \times d_k$ matrix by a $d_k \times m$ one, so the result is $n \times m$. Entry $(i,j)$ of it is the dot product of query row $i$ with key row $j$ — the [[compatibility-function|compatibility score]] for that query-key pair. One matrix product therefore produces all $n \times m$ scores at once, with no loop over pairs.

The next step is the scaling. Every entry of that score matrix is divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$.

The paper's footnote gives the reason, and the reason is about magnitude. Suppose the components of a query $q$ and a key $k$ are independent, each with mean $0$ and variance $1$. Their dot product is $q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$, a sum of $d_k$ such products, so it has mean $0$ and variance $d_k$.

The consequence is that scores spread further apart as $d_k$ grows. The authors suspect that large scores push [[softmax]] into regions with extremely small gradients. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ divides the variance by $d_k$, bringing it back to roughly $1$, and that division is exactly what the [[sqrt-dk-scaling|$1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor]] does. They state this as a suspicion, not a proof.

Softmax is then applied per row of the scaled $n \times m$ matrix, not over the whole matrix. Each row becomes non-negative weights that sum to $1$.

So each query ends up with its own distribution over the $m$ key-value pairs.

Multiplying by $V$ turns each of those weight rows into a weighted sum of value vectors. The result is $n \times d_v$: one output vector per query.

Strip the scaling out and what remains is exactly [[dot-product-attention|dot-product attention]], the standard variant. The paper prefers it over [[additive-attention|additive attention]] because it can be run as an optimized matrix multiplication.

In the base model this function is not run once but eight times in parallel, inside [[multi-head-attention|multi-head attention]]. The model width is [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]] and there are [[num-heads-h|$h = 8$]] heads, so each head works in $512/8 = 64$ dimensions. That makes $d_k = 64$, and $\sqrt{64} = 8$, so in the base model the divisor in Equation (1) is $8$.

terms.definition: The function being defined: it maps a set of queries plus a set of key-value pairs to one output vector per query. Each output is a weighted sum of value vectors.
The query matrix. Each row is one query vector of dimension $d_k$; the paper packs a whole set of queries into $Q$ so the attention function runs on all of them simultaneously.
The key matrix. Each row is one key vector of dimension $d_k$, advertising what the corresponding position holds so a query can match against it.
The value matrix. Each row is one value vector of dimension $d_v$, the content actually returned; the output is a weighted average of these rows.
The transpose of the key matrix. Transposing lets the single product $QK^T$ produce the dot product of every query with every key.
The matrix of raw compatibility scores: entry $(i,j)$ is the dot product of query $i$ with key $j$. Its shape is (number of queries) x (number of keys).
Applied to each row of the scaled score matrix: exponentiate the scores and divide by their sum, turning one query's scores into non-negative weights that sum to 1.
The dimension of the query and key vectors. It sets both the length of the dot product and, through $\sqrt{d_k}$, the scaling factor.
The dimension of the value vectors, and therefore of each output vector. It does not appear in the formula's scaling but determines the output width.
The divisor applied to every dot product before the softmax. It is the square root of the key dimension, chosen to cancel the growth of dot-product magnitude with dimension.
The scaling factor written as a multiplier in the surrounding text. The paper says this factor is the only difference between its attention and plain dot-product attention.
The paper's equation number for this formula; later sections refer back to it as equation (1).
The name the paper gives this particular attention function, distinguishing it from unscaled dot-product attention and from additive attention.
A single query vector and a single key vector, used in footnote 4's variance argument for why unscaled dot products grow large.
The dot product of one query with one key, $\sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$: a single entry of $QK^T$ before scaling.

numbers.meaning: The key and query dimension in the base model. It follows from the multi-head setup: $d_{model} = 512$ split across $h = 8$ heads gives $d_k = d_v = 512/8 = 64$.
The actual divisor in the base model: every query-key dot product is divided by 8 before the softmax.
Footnote 4's assumption about the components of $q$ and $k$: independent random variables with mean 0 and unit variance. This is an illustrative assumption, not a measured fact.

The result of footnote 4: under that assumption $q \cdot k$ has mean 0 and variance $d_k$, so the standard deviation is $\sqrt{d_k}$ — which is exactly what the equation divides by, restoring variance to about 1.
The equation number assigned to this formula in the paper.

items.caption: Multi-head attention / head_i
items.title: Attention in h parallel subspaces
items.takeaway: Instead of one attention function over full-width 512-dimensional vectors, the Transformer runs $h=8$ attention functions in parallel. Each one works on its own learned 64-dimensional projection of the queries, keys, and values. Their outputs are concatenated and projected once more. Because each head is narrower by a factor of $h$, the paper says the total computational cost stays similar to one full-width head.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at the definition of [[multi-head-attention|multi-head attention]]. It has three parts: two lines of math, and below them the shapes of the four learned matrices the math uses.

The two lines are easiest to read inside out, so start with the second one and work back up to the first.

$Q$, $K$, and $V$ are the [[queries-keys-values|query, key, and value]] matrices. Each has one row per sequence position. Each row is $d_{\text{model}}$ numbers wide.

The second line builds a single [[attention-head|head]]. It multiplies $Q$, $K$, and $V$ by three separate learned matrices, $W^Q_i$, $W^K_i$, and $W^V_i$, one set per head. Those multiplications shrink the three inputs into a lower-dimensional subspace belonging to that head. Then ordinary [[scaled-dot-product-attention|scaled dot-product attention]] runs on the shrunk versions, not on the originals.

The result is that head $i$ emits one $d_v$-dimensional vector for every position in the sequence.

Now the first line. It takes the $h$ heads' outputs and stacks them side by side — that is what Concat does — then multiplies the stacked result by a fourth learned matrix, $W^O$.

The [[attention-projection-matrices|shapes]] are what make that bookkeeping close. $W^Q_i$ and $W^K_i$ live in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}$, and $W^V_i$ lives in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}$, so all three map from model width down into a head's narrower space. Going the other way, concatenating $h$ heads of width $d_v$ produces $h d_v$ columns. That is why $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{h d_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$: it takes those $h d_v$ columns back to model width.

$W^O$ is doing more than a reshape. Up to that point each head has computed in isolation, on its own projection. $W^O$ is the only place where information from different heads mixes.

The sizing is the point of the whole construction. The base model uses [[num-heads-h|$h=8$]] heads and a model width of [[d-model|$d_{\text{model}}=512$]]. The paper divides the width evenly among the heads, so [[dk-dv-dimensions|each head gets $512/8 = 64$ dimensions for both keys and values]], giving $d_k = d_v = 64$.

Follow the cost through that division. A head operating at 64 dimensions instead of 512 does roughly $1/h$ of the work a full-width head would do. There are $h$ such heads running in parallel, and $h \times 1/h$ is 1. So the paper reports that the total cost is similar to that of single-head attention at full dimensionality.

Put plainly: on this accounting, extra heads are close to free compared with one wide head.

That leaves the question of why to split at all. The paper's answer is that multiple heads let the model attend jointly to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single head, it says, [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|averaging inhibits this]].

terms.definition: The multi-head attention function being defined: it takes the full-width queries, keys, and values and returns one $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional output vector per query position. It replaces a single attention call everywhere attention appears in the Transformer.
The queries: a matrix whose rows are the $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional vectors asking for information, one row per position that needs an output.
The keys: a matrix whose rows are $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional vectors, one per position that can be attended to, used to score how well each position matches a query.
The values: a matrix whose rows are the $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional contents retrieved from each attended position, averaged using the attention weights.
The output of the $i$-th parallel attention function: ordinary attention run on this head's own projected queries, keys, and values, producing one $d_v$-dimensional vector per position.
The head index, running from 1 to $h$. Each head has its own separate $W^Q_i$, $W^K_i$, $W^V_i$; nothing is shared between heads except the final $W^O$.
The number of parallel attention heads. In the base model $h = 8$.
Concatenation along the feature dimension: the $h$ head outputs, each $d_v$ wide, are laid side by side per position to form a single $h d_v$-wide vector.
The scaled dot-product attention function defined earlier in the paper: softmax of the query-key dot products divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$, used to weight the values.
The learned matrix that projects the full-width queries into head $i$'s query subspace; shape $d_{\text{model}} \times d_k$.
The learned matrix that projects the full-width keys into head $i$'s key subspace; shape $d_{\text{model}} \times d_k$. It must match $W^Q_i$'s output width so query-key dot products are defined.
The learned matrix that projects the full-width values into head $i$'s value subspace; shape $d_{\text{model}} \times d_v$. It sets the width of head $i$'s output.

The single learned output matrix applied after concatenation; shape $h d_v \times d_{\text{model}}$. It brings the stacked head outputs back to model width and is the only step that mixes information across heads.
The model width: the dimension of the vectors flowing between sub-layers, and the input and output width of multi-head attention. 512 in the base model.
The dimension of each head's projected queries and keys, i.e. the width of the space in which that head's dot products are taken. 64 here.
The dimension of each head's projected values, and therefore of that head's output vector. 64 here.
The width of the concatenated head outputs, and the number of rows of $W^O$. With $h = 8$ and $d_v = 64$ this equals 512.
Standard notation for the set of real matrices with $a$ rows and $b$ columns; used here only to state the shape of each projection matrix.

The lower-dimensional spaces that the projection matrices map into. The paper's stated motivation is that separate heads let the model attend jointly to information from different such subspaces at different positions.

numbers.meaning: The number of parallel attention layers, or heads, in the base model. The paper states this choice without deriving it; a later ablation reports that both fewer and many more heads score worse.
The model width: the input and output dimension of multi-head attention, fixed across the whole model so residual connections can add sub-layer inputs to outputs.

The per-head key/query and value dimension. It is set to the model width divided by the number of heads so that the concatenated heads come back out to exactly 512, and so that each head is $1/h$ as wide as a full-dimensional head.
The arithmetic behind the head width in the base model.
The row count of $W^O$: the width of the concatenated head outputs. Because it equals $d_{\text{model}}$, $W^O$ is a square 512 x 512 matrix in the base model.
The index range in the Concat: all $h$ heads are computed in parallel and all are concatenated, so head 1 through head 8 in the base model.

Each head owns $W^Q_i$, $W^K_i$, $W^V_i$, and one $W^O$ is shared; with $h = 8$ that is 25 learned matrices per multi-head attention sub-layer, though in practice the per-head projections are usually fused.

The paper's cost argument: because each head's dimension is reduced by the factor $h$, the total computational cost across all $h$ heads is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality.

items.caption: Position-wise feed-forward network, eq. (2)
items.title: The per-position feed-forward block
items.takeaway: Equation (2) defines the second sub-layer in every encoder and decoder layer: a two-layer MLP with a ReLU in between, applied to each position's vector on its own. It widens each 512-dimensional vector to 2048, rectifies, and projects back to 512. The weights are shared across positions but not across layers.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Equation (2) is the full definition of the [[position-wise-feed-forward-network|position-wise feed-forward network]]. This is the one [[sub-layer]] in the architecture that is not attention.

It appears in every layer of the [[encoder-stack|encoder]] and every layer of the [[decoder-stack|decoder]]. The paper describes it as "a fully connected feed-forward network, which is applied to each position separately and identically."

### How to read it

$x$ is one position's vector. Concretely, that is a single token's representation, of width [[d-model|$d_{\text{model}} = 512$]], arriving from the attention sub-layer below.

The formula reads left to right as three steps. Take them one at a time.

First, the affine map $xW_1 + b_1$. It takes the 512 numbers in $x$ and produces a wider vector, of the inner width [[d-ff|$d_{ff} = 2048$]]. That is four times the model width: $4 \times 512 = 2048$.

Second, $\max(0, \cdot)$. Applied entrywise, it zeroes every negative entry in those 2048 numbers and leaves the positive ones untouched. That operation is the [[relu|ReLU]], and it is the only nonlinearity in the block.

Third, $W_2$ and $b_2$ project the 2048 numbers back down to 512. So the output vector is exactly as wide as the input vector was.

The matching width is not incidental. Each sub-layer is wrapped in a [[residual-connection|residual connection]], which adds the sub-layer's input straight onto its output, and then in [[layer-normalization|layer normalization]]. That addition only typechecks if input and output are the same shape.

Now look at what the formula does *not* contain. There is no sum over positions and no second index $j$ anywhere in it.

Nothing here mixes tokens. In the [[transformer|Transformer]], all cross-position mixing happens in [[self-attention]] and [[multi-head-attention|multi-head attention]]. This block only reshapes each position on its own.

### What it shows

Two sharing rules, and they point in opposite directions.

Within a single layer, every position runs through the *same* $W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2$. One token's transformation is the transformation every token gets.

Across layers, the parameters differ. Each of the six encoder layers and each of the six decoder layers holds its own separate copy of the four parameter tensors.

The paper then offers a second reading of the very same computation: "two convolutions with kernel size 1."

Consider what a 1x1 convolution over a sequence does. Its kernel spans exactly one position, so it never sees a neighbor, and the kernel weights are the same wherever it is applied along the sequence.

That is precisely the sharing pattern described above — identical weights everywhere, no cross-position reach. The MLP view and the convolution view describe the same arithmetic, and which one you prefer is a matter of implementation habit.

terms.definition: The name the paper gives this function: the position-wise feed-forward network applied to a single position's vector x. It returns a vector of the same width as x.
The input to the block: one position's representation, a row vector of dimension d_model. In the encoder and decoder it is the output of the attention sub-layer directly below.
The first weight matrix, mapping from d_model = 512 up to the inner width d_ff = 2048. Written on the right of x, so x is treated as a row vector.
The bias vector added after the first linear map; it has d_ff = 2048 entries.
The second weight matrix, mapping the 2048-dimensional rectified hidden vector back down to d_model = 512.
The bias vector added after the second linear map; it has d_model = 512 entries.
Elementwise maximum against zero — the ReLU nonlinearity applied to the hidden vector. Negative entries become 0, non-negative entries pass through unchanged.
The rectified linear unit, the standard nonlinearity written here as max(0, ·). It is the only nonlinearity in this sub-layer; without it the two linear maps would collapse into one.
An affine map of the form (vector)(matrix) + (bias). The paper describes the block as "two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between."
The model's shared width, 512 in the base model. It is both the input and output dimension of this block, so the sub-layer can be dropped into a residual connection.
The width of the hidden (inner) layer inside this block, 2048 in the base model. Only W_1's output and W_2's input have this size.
One slot in the sequence — one token's vector. "Position-wise" means the block runs on each of these independently, with no information passing between them.
One of the N identical blocks in the encoder or decoder stack. Each layer contains attention sub-layer(s) plus one copy of this feed-forward network, with its own W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2.
A component inside a Transformer layer — either an attention mechanism or this feed-forward network — each wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization.
The half of the model that reads the input sequence; each of its layers contains self-attention followed by this feed-forward network.
The half of the model that generates the output sequence; each of its layers contains masked self-attention, encoder-decoder attention, and this feed-forward network.

A convolution whose window covers exactly one position. The paper says the block can equivalently be described as two such convolutions, since a 1x1 kernel applies the same weights at every position without mixing neighbors.
The paper's equation number for this formula, used to refer back to it elsewhere in the text.

numbers.meaning: d_model, the input and output dimension of FFN(x). The paper states "the dimensionality of input and output is d_model = 512"; it is the shared width of every sub-layer and embedding in the base model, which is what lets residual connections add sub-layer inputs to outputs.
d_ff, the dimensionality of the inner layer — the width after W_1 and before W_2. The paper states the value but does not argue for it here; it is four times d_model.
The ratio d_ff / d_model = 2048 / 512. Arithmetic from the two stated numbers; the paper does not comment on the ratio itself.
The threshold inside max(0, ·): the ReLU clamps every negative hidden unit to zero. It is a fixed constant, not a learned value.

Appears twice with different meanings. As the equation label "(2)" it is the paper's numbering. As a count, it is the number of linear transformations in the block — equivalently the number of kernel-size-1 convolutions in the alternative description.

Two roles. As the subscript in W_1 and b_1, it indexes the first linear transformation. As "kernel size 1", it is the width of the convolution window in the alternative reading — one position, so no neighboring positions are mixed.
The subscript in W_2 and b_2, indexing the second linear transformation — the projection from 2048 back to 512.

items.caption: Sinusoidal positional encoding pair
items.title: Position as a bank of sinusoids
items.takeaway: A model with no recurrence and no convolution has no idea what order its tokens are in. So the paper adds a fixed vector to each input embedding, whose entries are sines and cosines of the position at geometrically spaced wavelengths. The paper says it picked this over learned position vectors because relative offsets become linear functions of the encoding, and because it may extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen in training.
items.walkthrough:
This equation defines one [[positional-encoding|positional encoding]] vector: the vector that gets added to the token sitting at position $pos$. That vector has the same width as the token embeddings, $d_{model}$.

The two formulas are not two competing encodings. They are one vector, and each formula fills in half of its entries.

Read the subscript on $PE$ as a pair — (position, dimension). The first index, $pos$, picks out the token in the sequence: 0 for the first, 1 for the second, and so on. The second index picks out a slot inside the $d_{model}$-wide vector.

$i$ is the counter over those slots, and it moves two at a time. Entry $2i$ — the even slots — takes the sine. Entry $2i+1$ — the odd slots — takes the cosine.

Both use the same value of $i$, and therefore the same divisor inside the argument. So the vector's dimensions come in couples: a sine and a cosine sharing a single frequency. With $d_{model} = 512$ in the base model, $i$ runs from 0 up to 255, which gives 256 such couples. The paper's own phrasing is that "each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid."

What remains is the divisor, $10000^{2i/d_{model}}$, and it is the piece that sets one couple apart from the next. Work it at both ends.

Take the first couple, $i = 0$. The exponent $2 \cdot 0 / 512$ is 0, so the divisor is $10000^0 = 1$. The angle is then just $pos$ itself, and the sinusoid completes a full cycle every $2\pi$ positions — it turns over every few tokens.

Now the other end. As $i$ climbs toward $d_{model}/2$, which is 256 here, the exponent $2i/d_{model}$ approaches 1, so the divisor approaches $10000^1 = 10000$. Dividing $pos$ by ten thousand before taking the sine stretches the cycle by that same factor, to a wavelength of $10000 \cdot 2\pi$.

In between, the exponent steps up evenly, so the wavelengths grow by a constant multiplicative factor rather than by a constant amount. That is what the paper means when it describes the wavelengths as a geometric progression from $2\pi$ to $10000\cdot2\pi$.

The result is a division of labour across the vector. Low dimensions turn over quickly and carry fine position detail. High dimensions barely change from one token to the next, and instead separate distant regions of the sequence.

Two claims motivate choosing this construction over the alternative.

The first is about offsets. The paper hypothesized that this encoding makes attention by [[relative-position-linearity|relative position]] easy to learn, because for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$. The mechanism is the couple structure: within one sine/cosine pair, shifting the position by $k$ rotates that pair's two numbers by a fixed angle. There is one such rotation per pair, and none of them depends on $pos$. So a single linear map carries every position to the position $k$ steps ahead of it.

The second is about length. [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|The sinusoids]] are defined for any $pos$ — nothing in the formula requires having seen that position during training. On that basis the paper says the model "may" extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those in training.

The contrast there is with [[learned-positional-embedding|learned positional embeddings]], the obvious alternative: one trainable vector per position, learned like any other parameter. That scheme simply has no vector for a position it never saw.

The paper tried both. In its [[transformer-ablations|ablations]] the two gave nearly identical results (Table 3 row (E)).

One mechanical point closes this out. The encoding is summed with the [[token-embeddings|token embedding]], not concatenated onto it, and the addition happens once, at the bottom of both the [[encoder-stack|encoder]] and [[decoder-stack|decoder]] stacks.

Summing is why the encoding must be exactly $d_{model}$ wide. It has to line up entry for entry with the embedding it is added to.

terms.definition: The positional encoding: a table of fixed (non-learned) vectors, one per sequence position, added to the input embeddings so the model can use token order.
The value stored at even dimension 2i of the positional encoding vector for position pos. It is a sine.
The value stored at odd dimension 2i+1 of the positional encoding vector for position pos. It is a cosine at the same frequency as its partner at 2i.

The position of the token in the sequence — the paper says simply 'pos is the position'. It is the input to the sine and cosine, so shifting a token later in the sentence advances the phase of every sinusoid.
The dimension index within the encoding vector, which the paper calls 'the dimension'. It selects which sine/cosine pair you are computing, and therefore which frequency.
The shared width of the model — every embedding and sub-layer output is a vector of this size. The positional encoding has this same dimension so it can be summed with the embeddings.
The sine function, applied to the scaled position. It fills the even dimensions of the encoding.

The cosine function, applied to the same scaled position as its sine partner. It fills the odd dimensions. Having both means each frequency's contribution is a point on a circle, which is what makes an offset a rotation.
An arbitrary fixed offset between two positions, used in the paper's hypothesis: for any k, PE_{pos+k} can be represented as a linear function of PE_{pos}.
How many positions it takes for one sinusoid to complete a full cycle. Here wavelengths run from 2*pi in the lowest dimensions to 10000*2*pi in the highest.
Successive wavelengths are multiplied by a constant ratio rather than increased by a constant amount — the effect of putting i in the exponent of 10000.
The learned vectors that represent each token; the positional encoding is added to them at the bottom of the encoder and decoder stacks.
The alternative the paper tested: a trainable vector per position instead of a fixed formula. It gave nearly identical results but is undefined for positions beyond the training range.
The two halves of the Transformer. The positional encoding is added to the inputs at the bottom of both, not inside every layer.
The ablation row the paper points to as evidence that sinusoidal and learned positional encodings perform about the same.

numbers.meaning: The base of the frequency scale. Raising it to 2i/d_model sets the divisor for the position, so it fixes the ratio between the shortest and longest wavelength in the encoding. The paper does not justify this constant beyond the wavelength range it produces.
The even dimension indices of the encoding vector (0, 2, 4, ...), which hold sine values. The factor of 2 is what makes each frequency occupy a pair of adjacent dimensions.
The odd dimension indices (1, 3, 5, ...), which hold cosine values at the same frequency as the sine at 2i.
The exponent applied to 10000. It ranges from 0 (first dimension pair) to nearly 1 (last pair), so the divisor sweeps from 1 up to nearly 10000.
The shortest wavelength, at i = 0 where the divisor is 10000^0 = 1. The sinusoid completes a cycle every ~6.28 positions, encoding fine-grained position.

The longest wavelength, reached as 2i/d_model approaches 1 and the divisor approaches 10000. About 62,832 positions per cycle — over any realistic sentence this dimension barely changes, giving a slow, near-monotonic signal.
There are half as many distinct frequencies as dimensions, because each frequency uses two slots (one sine, one cosine).
The base model's width, stated elsewhere in the paper. The positional encoding must match it to be summed with the embeddings, giving 256 sine/cosine pairs.
The paper's claim holds for every fixed offset, not a particular one: PE_{pos+k} is a linear function of PE_{pos}, with the linear map depending on k but not on pos.

items.caption: Learning-rate schedule, eq. (3)
items.title: The warmup-then-decay learning rate
items.takeaway: Equation (3) makes the learning rate a function of the training step rather than a constant. It rises linearly for the first warmup_steps steps, then falls as the inverse square root of the step number, with the whole curve scaled by $d_{model}^{-0.5}$. The two branches meet at step = warmup_steps = 4000, and that crossover is where the rate peaks.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at the learning-rate schedule from Section 5.3. The learning rate here is not a fixed number chosen once and left alone.

It is recomputed at every training step. The value it produces is then handed to the [[adam-optimizer|Adam optimizer]], which the paper runs with [[transformer-adam-settings|$\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.98$, $\epsilon = 10^{-9}$]].

Read the formula inside-out, starting with the innermost piece. `step_num` is the current update count, and it starts at 1. The `min` around the two expressions picks whichever of them is smaller at that step:

- $step\_num \cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5}$ — a straight line through the origin. Since $warmup\_steps$ is a fixed constant, this term simply grows in proportion to the step count.
- $step\_num^{-0.5}$ — a decaying curve. Written out, it is $1/\sqrt{step\_num}$.

Early in training the line sits below the decay curve, so the `min` selects it and the rate climbs linearly. Later the decay term is the smaller of the two, so it takes over and the rate falls.

The handover point is easy to locate. Set the two expressions equal and solve, and you get $step\_num = warmup\_steps$.

So with the paper's setting the crossover sits exactly at step 4000. That crossover is also the peak of the whole schedule, because the rate is rising up to it and falling after it. Now the name for this shape can land: that linear ramp followed by inverse-square-root decay is what the [[learning-rate-warmup-schedule|warmup schedule]] refers to.

That covers the step-dependent part. The remaining factor, $d_{model}^{-0.5}$, does not depend on the step at all — it scales the entire curve up or down according to the model's width.

For the base model, [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]]. So the prefactor is $512^{-0.5} \approx 0.0442$. Because it is an inverse square root, wider models get proportionally smaller learning rates.

The two parts together give concrete numbers. At the peak, the schedule evaluates to $0.0442 \times 4000^{-0.5} \approx 7.0 \times 10^{-4}$. During the ramp, the rate grows by about $1.75 \times 10^{-7}$ per step.

What the equation shows is that the model is not trained at a constant rate. It starts near zero and works its way up before decaying.

The paper states this plainly and does not argue for warmup. It gives the formula, describes its shape, and reports [[warmup-steps-4000|warmup_steps = 4000]].

The common reading is worth separating from what the paper claims. Adam's second-moment estimate is unreliable in the first steps, when it has seen few gradients. With $\beta_2 = 0.98$, together with [[layer-normalization]] and [[residual-connection|residual connections]], large early steps can destabilize training. On that account, the ramp keeps the steps small until the estimates settle.

That rationale is not in the paper. Treat it as context, not as a claim the authors make.

The schedule is one component of the [[transformer-training-recipe|training recipe]], and it applies to both the base and the big models.

terms.definition: The learning rate handed to the optimizer at the current training step. It is recomputed every step rather than being a fixed hyperparameter.
The shared width of the model — every sub-layer and embedding outputs vectors of this dimension. It is 512 in the base Transformer, and it appears here only as a scaling factor on the learning rate.
The index of the current training step (parameter update), counting from 1. Both branches of the min are functions of it.
The number of initial steps over which the learning rate ramps up linearly. It also fixes where the peak sits, since the two branches cross at step_num = warmup_steps.

The two-argument minimum. It selects the linear ramp while the ramp is the smaller value (early training) and the inverse-square-root decay afterwards, producing one continuous curve with no explicit branch.
The gradient-descent variant this learning rate feeds. It adapts a per-parameter step size using running averages of the gradient and its square; the schedule scales those steps.
Adam's decay rate for the running average of the gradient (first moment). Set to 0.9 here, the standard value.
Adam's decay rate for the running average of the squared gradient (second moment). Set to 0.98 here, lower than Adam's usual 0.999, so the estimate tracks recent gradients more closely.
The small constant Adam adds to the denominator to avoid dividing by zero when the second-moment estimate is tiny. Set to 10^-9.
The first phase of the schedule, where the learning rate grows in proportion to the step number from near zero up to the peak.
The second phase, where the learning rate falls as 1/sqrt(step_num) — a slow decay with no fixed end point, so the schedule does not need to know the total training length in advance.
The paper's label for this formula, in Section 5.3 (Optimizer).

numbers.meaning: warmup_steps: the length of the linear ramp in training steps, and therefore the step at which the learning rate peaks. The paper states 'We used warmup_steps = 4000' without giving a derivation.
The exponent on the model width. It makes the learning rate scale as 1/sqrt(d_model), so wider models get proportionally smaller steps.

The decay exponent: after the peak the rate falls as the inverse square root of the step number, which the paper describes in words as 'decreasing it thereafter proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number'.
The exponent that sets the slope of the linear ramp. It is chosen so the ramp term equals the decay term exactly at step_num = warmup_steps, making the curve continuous at the peak.
